_comment: Diagnostic addenda appended to the prompt per species, upstream's mechanism for birds the model gets wrong. Each names the field marks that matter and the look-alike to avoid. Written for the four species the local list needs and the Australian sets do not have.
Corvus mellori: Little Raven. Entirely glossy black including bill, legs and feet - NO white, grey or pied markings anywhere. The iris is pale white-grey, the single most distinctive feature, and must read clearly against the black head. Throat hackles are short and inconspicuous, not the long shaggy beard of an Australian Raven. Bill is stout and moderately short with a gently curved culmen. Do NOT render this as a pied bird: Australian Magpie and Pied Currawong are different species in this same collection and any white wing or shoulder patch would make it one of them. Draw the body as FLAT colour - no scalloped feather outlines on the back, breast or belly, and no brown or bronze tint across the wing. At any normal viewing distance this bird shows no feather pattern at all. Structure only at the wing and tail edges.
Turdus merula: Eurasian Blackbird, adult male. Uniformly glossy jet-black plumage with a bright orange-yellow bill and a matching narrow orange-yellow eye-ring - those two warm features against flat black are the entire identity of this bird and must be unmistakable. Legs are dark brown, not yellow. NO white anywhere, no speckling, no pale wing panel. Medium thrush proportions with a fairly long tail, slim build, upright stance. Do NOT render the brown mottled female. Do NOT render a European Starling: no iridescent green-purple gloss, no pale spotting, no short square tail, no pointed pale bill. Draw the body as FLAT colour - no scalloped feather outlines on the back, breast or belly, and no brown or bronze tint across the wing. At any normal viewing distance this bird shows no feather pattern at all. Structure only at the wing and tail edges.
Acridotheres tristis: Common Myna. Rich chocolate-brown body and wings meeting a glossy BLACK head, throat and upper breast. The hood is BLACK -- not navy, not teal, not dark blue. A faint sheen is acceptable; a blue cast is not. The boundary where the black hood meets the brown breast is a CRISP EDGE, a hard line between two flat colours, NOT a soft gradient or a blended fade -- that sharp demarcation is diagnostic of the species and its absence makes the bird unrecognisable. A bare bright yellow patch of skin runs behind and below the eye. Bill and legs strong yellow. A bold WHITE wing patch on the primaries and a broad white tail tip, both clearly visible, especially in flight. CRITICAL: do NOT drift toward Noisy Miner, which is in this same collection and shares the yellow facial skin. A Noisy Miner is grey-bodied with a black crown and white forehead; the Common Myna is brown-bodied with an entirely black hood and white wing flashes. Body brown, not grey, and no pale forehead.
Anthochaera carunculata: Red Wattlebird. Large slim honeyeater, grey-brown above and below with dense fine WHITE STREAKING over the whole body - abstract this into two or three broad zones rather than rendering every streak. A pendulous fleshy pinkish-red wattle hangs from behind each eye down the side of the neck; this is the bird's name and must be clearly present. A bright yellow patch on the lower belly, and a white-tipped tail. Bill is fine, slightly downcurved, dark. Do NOT render a Little Wattlebird, which has no wattle and no yellow belly. Do NOT omit the wattle or the yellow belly patch.
Grallina cyanoleuca: Magpie-lark, adult male. NOT a magpie and not a corvid despite the name - a small slim mud-nester about the size of a starling, with long pink-grey legs and a pale ivory-white bill. Plumage is crisp BLACK AND WHITE in bold blocks, not the magpie's pattern: black crown and nape, a broad WHITE eyebrow stripe above a black face mask, white throat, white underparts, black breast band, black wings with a long white shoulder stripe. The eye is pale cream-white. Do not draw a heavy corvid bill, do not draw a solid black hood, and do not give it the Australian Magpie's white nape saddle.
Corvus tasmanicus: Forest Raven. Entirely glossy black including bill, legs and feet, with a white-grey iris. Heavier and stockier than the Little Raven, with a notably SHORT square-ended tail and a deep, thick bill. Draw the body as FLAT BLACK - no scalloped feather outlines on the back, breast or belly, because a real raven shows none at any normal viewing distance. Structure only at the wing and tail edges. The shaggy throat hackles are the one exception: a few bold pointed shapes at the throat, not soft texture.
Corvus coronoides: Australian Raven. Entirely glossy black including bill, legs and feet, with a white-grey iris. The diagnostic feature is the THROAT HACKLES: long pointed feathers hanging as a distinct shaggy beard below the bill, longer than any other Australian corvid. Long wings, long bill. Draw the body as FLAT BLACK - no scalloped feather outlines on the back, breast or belly. Structure only at the wing and tail edges, and the hackles.
Zosterops lateralis: Silvereye. Tiny warbler-like bird with a conspicuous ring of WHITE feathers encircling the eye - the single diagnostic mark, drawn as a clean white ring, not a smudge. Olive-green head and back, grey nape and mantle, buff flanks, pale throat, fine pointed dark bill.
Cacatua sanguinea: Little Corella. All-white cockatoo with NO yellow crest - do not give it the Sulphur-crested Cockatoo's yellow plume. Short blunt white crest usually held flat, a bare BLUE-GREY eye ring, and a salmon-pink wash between eye and bill. Stubby pale bill, grey legs. White does NOT mean uncoloured: paint the body in warm off-white and pale grey zones with clear ink edges, the way the Sulphur-crested Cockatoo and Great Egret in this collection are painted. Do not produce an uncoloured outline drawing, and do not outline every wing feather - a corella reads as a smooth white shape with a few wing edges.
Glossopsitta concinna: Musk Lorikeet. Mostly GREEN, not multicoloured - do not draw the Rainbow Lorikeet's blue head and orange breast. Bright red band across the forehead and through the eye, a yellow patch on the side of the breast, blue-grey crown wash, and a black bill tipped orange-red.
Anthochaera chrysoptera: Little Wattlebird. Like the Red Wattlebird but SMALLER and with NO red neck wattle and NO yellow belly patch - those are the Red Wattlebird's and must not appear. Dark grey-brown with fine white streaking, a rufous patch in the wing visible in flight, and a pale blue-grey patch of bare skin under the eye.
Fulica atra: Eurasian Coot. Sooty slate-grey body with a BLACKER head and neck, and the diagnostic white frontal shield running up the forehead above a white bill. Red eye. Large lobed grey-green feet. Build the body from two or three tonal zones - blacker head and neck against the slate-grey back and flank - not one flat fill. Vary the line weight the way a brush does; do NOT ring the whole bird in one uniform heavy outline, which reads as a modern vector sticker rather than a woodblock print. The white frontal shield and bill are the diagnostic feature and must survive the cut-out: paint them PALE IVORY-GREY, clearly darker than the cream paper, with a firm ink outline all the way round. Not bare paper, not the paper's own colour.
Strepera versicolor: Gray Currawong. Large dark SOOTY GREY bird - grey, not black - with a heavy black bill and a bright YELLOW iris. The WHITE is diagnostic and must be present: a clear WHITE PATCH in the wing, a broad WHITE TIP to the tail, and WHITE undertail coverts. Without that white this bird is indistinguishable from the three ravens in this same collage (Little Raven, Australian Raven, Forest Raven), which are glossy black with a white-grey iris and NO white plumage - do not produce a fourth raven. It is also NOT the Pied Currawong, which is blacker and carries a WHITE RUMP BAND; the Gray Currawong has no rump band. Long heavy bill, long tail, sturdy dark legs.
Coracina novaehollandiae: Black-faced Cuckooshrike. Slim medium bird in GREY, BLACK AND WHITE ONLY. The grey is a PALE, LIGHT, SILVERY NEUTRAL GREY - the overall impression is of a PALE bird, close to the grey of weathered galvanised wire, not a dark one. It must NOT be blue-grey, slate, steel-blue, teal or blue-green: no blue or green cast at all. Do not darken it toward charcoal; the body should read clearly LIGHTER than the black mask and only a little darker than the white belly. Pale silvery grey covers the crown, nape, back and breast; the BELLY and undertail are WHITE, with a soft transition from grey breast to white belly. A solid BLACK FACE MASK covers the forehead, lores, chin, throat and ear-coverts, ending in a clean edge against the grey breast. Wings are darker grey to blackish with fine pale grey feather edges; the tail is dark with a white tip. Stout slightly hooked BLACK bill, dark legs. There is NO rufous, chestnut, brown, orange or buff anywhere on this bird - not on the wing coverts, not on the shoulder, not on the flanks.
Phylidonyris novaehollandiae: New Holland Honeyeater. Boldly BLACK-AND-WHITE STREAKED over the whole body - a black ground broken by dense white streaking on breast, belly and flanks, never a plain back. The WHITE IRIS is the single most diagnostic feature and must read clearly against the black face. Bright YELLOW PANELS in the folded and spread wing, with yellow edging in the tail. Small white tuft at the base of the bill and a fine white eyebrow. Slender decurved black bill. There is NO red, orange or pink on the face and NO rufous or brown on the back - do not drift toward a red-faced or brown-backed honeyeater. Distinguish from the White-plumed and Yellow-faced Honeyeaters in this same collage, which are plain olive and unstreaked. Draw ONE bird only, never a pair.
Cacatua tenuirostris: Long-billed Corella. White cockatoo. THE BILL is the identity and it is unmistakably a COCKATOO's bill - the same deep, rounded, heavy base and the same overhanging hooked tip as the Little Corella and Sulphur-crested Cockatoo already in this set - just with the hook drawn out somewhat longer. Build it in two parts: (1) a DEEP, BROAD, rounded base at the face, with a short blunt LOWER MANDIBLE clearly visible beneath it; (2) the upper mandible curving down and forward past that lower mandible into a tapering point. LENGTH: that projecting point is only MODERATELY long - roughly the same length as the bill is deep at its base, so the whole bill reaches forward about HALF the length of the head. It is NOT as long as the head, NOT a sickle, NOT a scimitar, and NOT a long smooth even curve. Err SHORT rather than long: a slightly stubby bill is a far smaller error than a wader's bill. The silhouette must never resemble an ibis, hornbill, curlew or any bird that probes mud. Colour is GREY to blue-grey horn - not white, not ivory, not black or brown. Bare BLUE-GREY skin surrounds the eye - skin, not a brightly coloured iris. An orange-red patch runs between eye and bill, and a broad ORANGE-RED CRESCENT crosses the throat and upper breast. The crest is SHORT, white and lies flat on a rounded head - no raised yellow plume. STANCE: standing UPRIGHT on its feet, body compact and held high, head up, exactly as the Little Corella in this set stands. The tail is SHORT and SQUARE. Do NOT draw a low-slung, crouching or prone bird, do NOT stretch the body out long and horizontal like a pigeon's, and do NOT give it a long tapering tail. GREY legs and feet, never brown. White does NOT mean uncoloured: paint the body in warm off-white, pale grey and faint pink zones with clear ink edges.
Psephotus haematonotus: Red-rumped Parrot, adult male. Bright emerald-green head, nape and breast shading to a clear YELLOW belly, with blue-green wings and a long graduated blue-green tail. The diagnostic mark is a single BRICK-RED patch on the RUMP, seen from above at the base of the tail. Slender pale grey-black bill, grey legs. Draw exactly ONE bird, with exactly ONE PAIR of wings and ONE red rump patch: do not duplicate the wings, the body or the rump patch into a second overlapping bird, and do not add extra wing masses behind the first pair.
